name: Kuikuro
confidence_why: Becker, Franchetto, Kuikuro, Kuikuro and Petrovic (2025) describe Kuikuro word stress as left-to-right iambs with a final trochee so that the penult carries the default prominence, and the only other first-hand description, Basso's (2019) Kalapalo grammar with stress on the second syllable from the left, covers the sister variety that da Silva and Franchetto (2011) show has a distinct prosodic system, so the penultimate rule for Kuikuro rests on a single modern source and no contradiction.
catalog_citation: Becker, Michael, Bruna Franchetto, Arawa Didi Kuikuro, Yanapa Mehinaku Kuikuro & Andrija Petrovic. 2025. The incoherent stress of Kuikuro. Natural Language & Linguistic Theory 43: 2363-2393. doi:10.1007/s11049-025-09676-2 (author-posted publisher PDF, becker.phonologist.org).
catalog_locator: Author-posted publisher PDF (31 pp., journal pagination not printed): Abstract and §1 opening sentence; §1, paragraph after Fig. 3; §3 preamble; §3.1 'Default and lexical length in verbs', paragraph following Table 2; §3.6 'Local summary'; §4 preamble; §4.1 'Final shortening is phrasal', first two paragraphs for the non-phrase-final stress statement; §5 'Lexical tone'; §7 'Conclusions'.
catalog_quote: Regardless of the number of syllables in the word, the default phrasal High tone docks on the head of the rightmost foot. Assuming a final trochee allows us to derive two generalizations: (1) the lack of lengthening and (2) the position of the High tone, which uniformly docks on the penultimate stressed syllable. Here and throughout, a stressed syllable is defined as the head syllable of a foot, and the primary stress of a word is defined as the head of the head foot of the word. [...] High tones appear by default on the penultimate syllable regardless of vowel length. We derive this pattern by making three assumptions: first, when the left-to-right iambic parse leaves two short vowels at the right edge, they are footed into a trochee (trochaic reversal). Second, we assume that the last foot of the word is the head foot of the word, and third, that a High tone is assigned to the head syllable of the head foot of the word. The combination of trochaic reversal and right-headedness together ensure that the penult is the head of the word. [...] Unlike phrase-final words, which have uniform penultimate stress by default, stress in non-phrase-final words is variable: the primary stress is penultimate in odd-parity words, e.g., [(ihũ:)bE] ‘coal’, and final in even-parity words.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Feet are iambs built left to right: even-numbered non-final vowels are rhythmically lengthened (lexically long vowels always head a foot and restart the count; long vowels are shortened phrase-finally). If two short syllables remain at the right edge they form a trochee; otherwise a single leftover final syllable is unparsed. The rightmost foot is the head foot, so in a word in isolation the primary stress is always the penult, which carries a default High tone; the lengthened even-numbered syllables to its left are secondary (foot-head) stresses. In multi-word phonological phrases the phrase is left-headed: the primary stress of the phrase is the primary stress of the first word, non-initial words lose their tone, and the single High tone is realized at the right end of a domain running from that stressed syllable up to (not including) the next foot head, so the pitch peak can sit up to three syllables after the stressed syllable ('incoherent' stress).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: heads of the non-final iambs, i.e. rhythmically lengthened even-numbered syllables counted from the left (and any lexically long vowel), e.g. [(ala:)(makí:)lɨ] 's/he fell', [(tʃiha:)(lama:)(kílɨ)] 'we fell' (§1, §3.1, Table 1).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexically long vowels (a minority of roots, 17/59 verb roots) disrupt the iambic count but not the penult primary stress; nouns, adjectives and postpositions (not verbs) may bear lexical High tone on the final or antepenultimate syllable, which replaces the default penult tone in isolation (e.g. [(takí)] 'cricket', [(á:)(dʒahi)] 'potoo'; 72% of 119 personal names have final lexical tone; Portuguese loans keep tone on the Portuguese stressed syllable); monosyllables keep long vowels ([(í:)] 'tree'); phrase-medially a word-initial onsetless short vowel is left unparsed, shifting the count; vocatives shift final tone leftward and echo questions add a final H, so root-final lexical tone on common nouns varies between [(táki)] and [(takí)] in citation forms (§5, §7).
new_statements.domain_note: Statement is for words in isolation (= one-word phonological phrases, citation forms); primary stress defined as head of the head (final) foot. In multi-word phrases only the first word keeps its tone and the H peak may be displaced rightward from the stressed syllable; vowel-length (footing) evidence for stress remains word-internal. Data from original fieldwork with two Kuikuro-speaking coauthors (Ipatse village variety).
new_statements.identity_note: Becker et al. 2025 describe the Kuikuro variety (Ipatse and neighbouring villages) of what Franchetto treats as one Upper Xingu Carib language with two dialects, Kuikuro/Matipu vs Kalapalo/Nahukwá; Glottolog kuik1246 'Kuikúro-Kalapálo' covers both. The stress statement should be attributed to the Kuikuro dialect only: Becker et al. say the Kalapalo foot type is 'unknown, but.. suggests that it is iambic', and Silva & Franchetto 2011 show Kalapalo phrase-level prominence patterns differ from Kuikuro's.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog row (penultimate stress = penultimate) and the existing statement (Becker et al. 2025: L-to-R iambs with final trochaic reversal, default H tone on the penult) are for the Kuikuro variety. Basso's grammar describes the Kalapalo variety of the same Glottolog languoid and places primary stress on the second syllable from the left (first in disyllables): identical to the catalog for 2- and 3-syllable words (10, 010) but different from the penult for 4+ syllables (Basso: 0100, 01000.; catalog: 0010, 00010..). Basso's Kalapalo pattern is what a left-aligned iamb would give, matching Becker et al.'s own conjecture (p. 30 of their PDF) that 'Kalapalo might have iambic footing as in Kui…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the second syllable from the left in words of three or more syllables (with falling intonation after it and no further stress); disyllables are stressed on the first syllable; monosyllables are stressed. Basso states (p. 25) that 'the language rhythm is stress-based rather than achieved through syllable weight', so no weight sensitivity. Described for the Kalapalo variety.
new_statements.secondary_stress: §2.3.2, p. 33: 'in complex phonological words, primary stress remains on the second syllable. However, units with more than six syllables have secondary stress (usually at morphological boundaries), followed by falling intonation, and no other stress on subsequent syllables.' Secondary stress also arises where clitic strings (1-5 syllables) follow a longer host, and on a normally unstressed syllable emphasized for pragmatic reasons; example u'iŋ.Gu.Gi-''ta=ki'ŋi'a.le'feke: with primary ('), secondary ('') and emphatic clause-final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 28: 'There are several kinds of exceptions to the basic stress pattern of primary second syllable stress on polysyllabic (3 syllables or more) words. These include: words beginning with the pronominal prefix, demonstrative words, the dative case marker -iña, imperative constructions where the speaker uses the interrogative mirative suffix -ki, and in discourse segments wherein the nominal is emphasized but not topicalized for pragmatic reasons'. Detail: pronominal-prefixed verbs and possessed nouns normally get primary stress on the third syllable because the prefix may itself be stressed (§2.3.1.2, p. 29); pronominal demonstratives stressed on first or second syllable, adnominal/identificational demonstratives on the second (§2.3.1.3); imperatives stressed on the first syllable (§2.3.1.4, p. 29-30); rising intonation with interrogatives and mirative -ki (§2.3.1.5); personal names vary, e.g. some with penultimate stress (§2.3.1.6); boundary-marking suffixes lengthen and stress the preceding syllable, shifting word stress rightward, e.g. 'ai.fa vs ai'fa:? (§2.3.1.7, pp. 31-32); pragmatic/emphatic stress including heavy clause-final stress (§2.3.1.8); Portuguese loans keep source-language stress, e.g. melan'zía (penult), só:gro (initial) (§2.3.3, p. 33).
new_statements.identity_note: Basso's grammar describes Kalapalo (ISO kui; Glottolog places Kalapalo under kuik1246 Kuikuro-Kalapalo), spoken by the Kalapalo and Nahukwa; Basso herself notes (ch. 2, p. 10-11) that Franchetto treats Kalapalo as a subdialect of 'Kuikuro'. The catalog row and the Becker et al. 2025 statement are for the Kuikuro variety proper (Kuikuro + Matipu/Uagihütü dialect group). The two dialect groups are documented as prosodically distinct (da Silva & Franchetto 2011; DoBeS Kuikuro project page), so the fixed: second syllable statement should be attached to the Kalapalo dialect, and the fixed: penultimate syllable catalog rule kept for Kuikuro.

tone_statements.citation: Franchetto, Bruna. 1986. Falar Kuikúro: estudo etnolinguístico de um grupo karíbe do Alto Xingu. Tese de doutorado, Museu Nacional/UFRJ, 605 pp.
tone_statements.quote: O acento tônico é o fator mais importante do sistema entoacional Kuikúro. É preciso antecipar aqui aspectos da língua que serão tratados no Cap. 3 e na Introdução ao Apêndice. Distinguem-se os níveis (a) da palavra isolada e (b) do enunciado, pois o acento tem funções sintáticas. (a) O acento é geralmente na penúltima sílaba da raiz (1), deslocando-se quando esta recebe sufixos (1a e 1b), e o tom sobe na sílaba tônica.
tone_statements.translation: Stress is the most important factor of the Kuikuro tonal and intonational system. ... Two levels are distinguished, (a) the isolated word and (b) the utterance, since stress has syntactic functions. (a) Stress is generally on the penultimate syllable of the root (1), shifting when the root takes suffixes (1a, 1b), and the pitch rises on the stressed syllable.
tone_statements.locator: Vol. I, Cap. 2, Secao 3, 'KUIKURO', p. 87; cf. Apendice III 'Acento', app. pp. 3-4
tone_statements.summary: No lexical tone posited: pitch ('tom') rises on the stressed syllable (penult of the root) and the 'grupo tonal' is an intonational unit; stress itself is called non-phonemic.

readall_conflicts: The single work opened, Basso 2019 (ch. 2, §2.3.1, pp. 27-28), gives second-syllable-from-the-left primary stress for polysyllables (initial in disyllables) for the Kalapalo variety, whereas the catalog and Becker et al. 2025 give default penultimate prominence for the Kuikuro variety. The two coincide for 2- and 3-syllable words and diverge for longer words. This is a known dialect difference rather than a factual contradiction about one system: da Silva & Franchetto 2011 (already held by the project, pp. 48-51) show Kuikuro and Kalapalo differ both acoustically (Kuikuro F0 only; Kalapalo F0 plus duration) and in where the prominent syllable falls relative to the [argument#head] merge, and Becker et al. 2025 explicitly leave Kalapalo footing open, suggesting left-aligned tone. Within Basso's own work there is a smaller inconsistency noted earlier for mati1253: her 1988/1995 books say the same as the 2019 grammar (disyllables initial, longer words second syllable), while a 1987/1992 book-chapter note says 'stress is normally on the penultimate syllable'; the 2019 grammar, being the fullest and latest statement, supersedes that note. Basso's description is impressionistic (no instrumental data), unlike Becker et al. and da Silva & Franchetto.

sources.note: Full word- and phrase-level analysis: left-to-right iambs with rhythmic lengthening of even-numbered vowels, lexical long vowels disrupt the count, final long vowels banned phrase-finally, final trochaic reversal; last foot is the head foot, so the penult of a word in isolation is uniformly the primary stress and carries a default High tone; in phrases the H-tone domain starts at the primary stress of the first word and may surface up to three syllables to the right ('incoherent' stress). Nouns/adjectives/postpositions may carry lexical tone (final or antepenult); verbs do not.

tone.translation: These variants are distinguished by lexical differences and, specifically, by different prosodic structures, having one and the same syntax. … the rhythmic (or melodic) differences are indices of the identities of the Carib groups. … The main pitch accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Heavy final syllables (nasalized and diphthongized) attract the accent. The rhythmic structure builds moraic trochees from right to left

tone.quote: O acento de altura geralmente cai na penúltima sílaba da palavra. Sílabas finais pesadas (nasalizadas e ditongos) atraem o acento.
tone.translation: The pitch accent generally falls on the penultimate syllable of the word. Heavy final syllables (nasalized ones and diphthongs) attract the accent.
tone.summary: Brief sketch after Franchetto and Santos: the word accent is called a pitch accent (acento de altura), usually penultimate, drawn to heavy final syllables; lexical tone is not discussed.
